_doc: Light-artillery detachment, commands, loading sequence, limber/caisson positions, prolonge use and rates of fire. FINDING: Gibbon's Artillerist's Manual (1860) does NOT contain the detachment drill - it says 'The manner of loading ... being given in the tactics' (item ART-GB-01). The drill is therefore taken from the 1860 Light Artillery Board's 'Instruction for Field Artillery' (1863 printing, archive.org cu31924030759330, acquired under the single extra-fetch allowance); Gibbon supplies rates of fire, canister effect, prolonge discussion and recoil theory. The manual is the Union (US Army) system; Confederate practice drew on the same Gibbon/Barry/Anderson tradition but this file proves nothing about Confederate crew size. Every item: manual id, printed page (OCR-recovered, confidence stated), verbatim OCR phrase (<15 words, code-verified), paraphrase. Tier documented unless stated.

detachment_summary.size: Nine men including the gunner (gunner + Nos. 1-8), chief of piece separate. No. 8 is the chief of the caisson, stationed 4 yd behind the limber; the PDF engine rule (8 at the piece + chief of caisson as a ninth) matches the manual's count of nine if "chief of caisson" is No. 8.

chief of piece.duty: sergeant in charge of the piece (manual: stands opposite the middle of the trail handspike, moves to see the fall of shot); repeats commands

gunner.duty: end of trail handspike; gives executive commands; points (direction by handspike, elevation by hausse/elevating screw); orders Ready/Fire; sends fuze time to No. 6

No. 1.duty: right of the muzzle, 2 ft outside the wheel; sponges (watching the vent) and rams

No. 2.duty: left of the muzzle; receives the round from No. 5 and puts it in the muzzle (seam clear of the vent); takes charge of ammunition when drawing a load

No. 3.duty: right side by the cascable; serves (thumb-stalls) the vent, shifts the trail on the gunner's tap, pricks the cartridge

No. 4.duty: left side by the cascable; lanyard hooked to a friction primer, inserts the primer, pulls on "Fire"

No. 5.duty: 5 yd behind the left wheel; carries single rounds from the limber to No. 2

No. 6.duty: behind the limber chest; issues rounds, cuts fuzes for shell/case to the time the gunner sends

No. 7.duty: left, near the left limber wheel; assists No. 6 (fuzes, passing rounds); with No. 6 draws the limber by hand

No. 8 (chief of caisson).duty: 4 yd behind the limber on its left; serves ammunition direct from the caisson rear chest doing No. 6's duties

summary: Gunner points; No. 3 shifts the trail
Prime: No. 3 pricks, No. 4 inserts the primer
Run up if necessary; sponge again
loading_sequence.note: The manual's order is: Load (sponge, load, ram, point) - Ready (prick, insert tube) - Fire. The PDF's list (sponge, load, ram, prime, point, fire) differs only in the point/prime order: the manual points before priming. Worm use after firing is only in drawing a load (para 477), not in each cycle (PDF/CVBT's "No. 2 with worm staff after firing" is not supported here).

ammunition_differences.summary: Shot: strapped shot (cartridge, ball, sabot) rammed after sponging; canister: no fuze, same crew, begins at 350 yd (double canister at 150-160 yd); shell and spherical case: No. 6 cuts the fuze to the time the gunner sends, No. 5 shows the cut fuze to the gunner before handing it to No. 2, not used at advancing bodies; case not inside 500 yd. Howitzer shell: fuze toward the rammer head.

items.verbatim: No. 1 goes through all his duties at the command Load,

items.paraphrase: No. 1 (right side): until "Load" stands square to the front in line with the front of the wheels, sponge held at its middle in the right hand trailing at 45 degrees. At "Load": faces left, steps obliquely right, brings the sponge upright; two: steps left to opposite the muzzle; three: side-steps 30 in. right, bends the right knee, sponge horizontal with the head against the muzzle; four: inserts the sponge head and forces it home.

items.paraphrase: "Sponge": No. 1 watches that the vent is closed, gives the sponge two turns pressing it to the bottom of the bore, draws it out, turns it end for end and, as No. 2 inserts the charge, enters the rammer head in the muzzle. During sponging No. 1 keeps his eye on the vent; if it is not closed he stops the drill and commands "stop vent".
items.verbatim2: No. 1 fixes his eye on the vent to see that it is closed,
items.verbatim: Sponge. 3 pauses ; 4 motions.

items.paraphrase: "Ram": No. 1 rams home throwing his weight on the rammer (bending over the left knee, left arm over the piece toward the left trunnion, right shoulder back and eyes to the front), then jerks the sponge/rammer out and steps back outside the wheel, sponge upright on the right toe.
items.verbatim2: No. 1 rams home, throwing the weight of his body with the rammer
items.verbatim: Ram. 2 pauses ; 3 motions.

items.paraphrase: Reason for the posture in ramming (left hand joined to right, eyes to the front, right shoulder refused): to guard against fatal results of a premature discharge.
items.verbatim: guard against fatal results in case of a premature discharge.

items.paraphrase: "Ready": No. 1 breaks well off to his left, left knee bent, right leg straight, sponge/rammer held horizontal in both hands, eyes on the muzzle; after the shot he rises on the right knee and returns to his post.

items.paraphrase: Limbering to the front ("Limber to the front"): No. 1 passes the sponge on its hook to No. 3 who keys it; the piece is brought about by hand (gunner and No. 5 on the trail, Nos. 1-2 on the muzzle, Nos. 3-4 on the wheels); the limber passes to its place; the gunner commands "Halt, limber up" and the lunette is run onto the pintle and keyed.

items.paraphrase: "Fix prolonge to fire retiring": the limber inclines right, wheels left about and halts 4 yards from the trail; No. 5 uncoils the prolonge and passes the toggle to the gunner who fixes it through the trail lunette while the other end is ringed over the limber pintle and keyed.

items.paraphrase: "Fix prolonge to fire advancing": the limber passes the piece on the right and halts in front, No. 5 carries the prolonge to the front, No. 2 puts the toggle in the axle-strap lunette; at "Halt" No. 2 takes out the toggle and commands "Drive on" and the limber returns to its place behind.

items.paraphrase: The prolonge is used when artillery retires slowly; the manual adds that cavalry will hesitate to attack a column retiring with the prolonge if its flank is secure. Wheels can also be locked with the prolonge.

items.verbatim: The prolonge should be generally used when artillery is retiring slowly.

items.paraphrase: Gibbon: grape/canister gives good results at 300-600 yd with maximum effect at 400-450 yd; fired too close the balls bunch, too far they spread; low fire over hard dry ground can use ricochet; 12-pdr spherical case effective up to 800 yd.
items.verbatim2: 12-pound schrapnell are effective up to 800 yards.
items.verbatim: the maximum effect is produced at from 400 to 450 yards.

items.paraphrase: Gibbon's free-recoil calculation: a piece only about 100 times heavier than its shot (as with the 12-pdr field gun, 121 times) would recoil 17.4 ft if unchecked, enough to destroy the carriage unless the charge is reduced "and in field artillery this is done". This is a theoretical free-recoil figure (no ground friction), NOT a measured carriage roll-back; no measured recoil distance appears in any of the texts.

items.paraphrase: Fuze: the Bormann (Belgian) metallic time fuze is the only kind used in field artillery; a 1.5 in. disc with a circular composition groove, graduated in seconds and fractions up to 5.5 s, the cover cut with the fuze-cutter/gouge to expose the composition to the discharge flame; two cutters per piece.

items.paraphrase: Friction primer: small tube filled with rifle powder inserted in the vent at the moment of firing, ignited by drawing a rough wire through a friction composition (1 part potassium chlorate to 2 antimony sulphide) with a lanyard; the number of primers issued is 50 per cent above the number of rounds.
items.verbatim2: friction primers is fifty per cent, greater than the number of rounds
items.verbatim: filled with rifle powder and inserted in the vent at the moment of firing.
